questions.question: What is the primary reason for replicating data across multiple database servers?
options: To make write operations faster
To provide fault tolerance and improve read scalability
To eliminate the need for backups
To avoid using indexes
questions.explanation: Replication creates copies of data on multiple machines so that if one fails, others can serve requests. It also lets you spread read queries across replicas for better performance.

questions.question: In leader-follower replication, which node accepts write operations?
options: Any follower can accept writes
Only the leader accepts writes
Writes are distributed evenly across all nodes
A randomly selected node handles each write
questions.explanation: In leader-follower (also called primary-replica) replication, all writes go to the leader. The leader then replicates changes to followers, which serve read-only queries.

questions.question: Replication lag refers to:
options: The time it takes to write data to the leader
The delay between a write on the leader and that write appearing on a follower
The time it takes to promote a follower to leader
Network latency between the client and the load balancer
questions.explanation: Replication lag is the time difference between when the leader processes a write and when that write is applied on a follower. During this window, followers may serve stale data.

questions.question: The 'read-your-writes' consistency guarantee ensures that:
options: All users see writes immediately
A user who made a write will always see that write in subsequent reads
Writes are synchronously replicated before acknowledgment
Followers never serve stale data
questions.explanation: Read-your-writes (also called read-after-write) consistency guarantees that if a user writes data, their own subsequent reads will reflect that write — even if other users might still see stale data.

questions.question: During leader failover, the most common strategy is to promote:
options: The follower with the oldest data
A brand new empty server
The follower that is most caught up with the leader's writes
All followers simultaneously to be co-leaders
questions.explanation: During failover, the follower closest to the leader's latest state is promoted. This minimizes data loss since it has replicated the most recent writes.

questions.question: A write-ahead log (WAL) in the context of replication is:
options: A log of all read queries for auditing
An append-only record of every change, streamed to followers for replay
A configuration file for replication settings
A temporary cache of uncommitted transactions
questions.explanation: The WAL records every database change in order. The leader streams this log to followers, which replay the entries to reproduce the exact same data changes.

questions.question: In synchronous replication, a write is acknowledged to the client:
options: As soon as the leader receives it
Only after at least one follower has confirmed it received the write
After all followers and the leader have flushed to disk
Before the leader even processes it
questions.explanation: Synchronous replication waits for at least one follower to confirm it has the write before acknowledging success to the client. This guarantees the data exists on multiple nodes but adds latency.

questions.question: The main trade-off of asynchronous replication compared to synchronous is:
options: It's slower but more durable
It's faster but risks data loss if the leader crashes before replication
It requires more followers
It doesn't support failover
questions.explanation: Async replication acknowledges writes immediately on the leader without waiting for followers. This is faster, but if the leader crashes before shipping a write, that write is lost.

questions.question: In a quorum-based system with 5 replicas, how many nodes must acknowledge a write for it to be considered successful (using majority quorum)?
questions.explanation: A majority quorum requires more than half of the nodes: ceil(5/2) = 3. With 3 acknowledgments, the write is guaranteed to overlap with any subsequent quorum read.

questions.question: Split-brain in leader-follower replication occurs when:
options: A follower falls too far behind the leader
Two nodes both believe they are the leader and accept conflicting writes
The leader runs out of disk space
Replication lag exceeds a configured threshold
questions.explanation: Split-brain happens during a network partition when a follower is promoted to leader while the old leader is still running. Both accept writes, causing data conflicts that are difficult to resolve.
